citation.authors: Trenton Bricken, Adly Templeton, Joshua Batson, Brian Chen, Adam Jermyn (core contributors) et al.; correspondence Chris Olah
citation.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning

verification_method: Fetched 2026-10-20. The page is 20.6 MB (embedded figures), which exceeded WebFetch's size limit, so it was downloaded with curl and the text extracted with a stdlib Python script that strips script, style and svg elements. All quotes are verbatim from that text. Figures are not readable in the extracted text, so numbers that only appear in plots (e.g. the distribution of automated correlation scores) are marked unverifiable below.

claims.planned: Features from a sparse autoencoder on a one-layer transformer were judged by a blinded human annotator with a rubric, sampling across the activation spectrum rather than top examples only
claims.finding: One author (Adam Jermyn) scored features and neurons blind, using a rubric covering confidence in an explanation, consistency of activations, consistency of logit output weights, and specificity. Samples were drawn uniformly from 11 activation intervals between 0 and the maximum activation, explicitly to avoid the top-example weakness of prior work. 412 feature-activation intervals were scored across 162 features and neurons.
claims.quote: At present, we do not have any metric we trust more than human judgment of interpretability. Thus, we had a blinded annotator (one of the authors, Adam Jermyn) score features and neurons based on how interpretable they are. ... In doing this evaluation, we wanted to avoid a weakness we perceived in our prior work (e.g., ) of focusing evaluation predominantly on maximal dataset examples, and paying less attention to the rest of the activation spectrum. Many polysemantic neurons appear monosemantic if you only look at top dataset examples, but are revealed to be polysemantic if you look at lower parts of the activation spectrum. ... In total, 412 feature activation intervals were scored across 162 features and neurons.
claims.location: Global Analysis > How Interpretable is the Typical Feature? > Manual Human Analysis

claims.planned: Human rubric result: median neuron scored 0, median feature interval scored 12
claims.finding: As stated; rubric maximum is 14 according to the essay by Cammarata that cites this result (the extracted text here gives the subjective 'above 8' threshold, 0 and 12).
claims.quote: Very subjectively, we found features to be quite interpretable if their rubric value was above 8. The median neuron scored 0 on our rubric, indicating that our annotator could not even form a hypothesis of what the neuron could represent! Whereas the median feature interval scored a 12, indicating that the annotator had a confident, specific, consistent hypothesis that made sense in terms of the logit output weights.

claims.planned: Automated interpretability followed Bills et al.: Claude writes an explanation from activating examples, then predicts activations on previously unseen tokens, with no leak of activation information except the explanation
claims.finding: Confirmed, with the explicit no-leak statement. Scoring uses Spearman correlation over 60 examples of nine tokens each (540 predictions per feature); half the scoring examples come from across the activation intervals rather than purely random text. Explanations were generated by Claude 2 from 49 examples kept separate from the 60 prediction examples; activations quantized 0-9 as in Bills et al. The appendix adds that Pearson correlation gives almost identical distributions.
claims.quote: Following the approach of Bills et al. , we have a large language model, Anthropic's Claude, generate explanations of features using examples of tokens where they activate. Next, we have the model use that explanation to predict new activations on previously unseen tokens. It's worth explicitly stating that our automated interpretability setup was designed to ensure that there's no leak of information about activation patterns, except for the explanation. For example, when predicting new activations, the model cannot see any true activations of that feature. ... Concretely, for each feature, we computed the Spearman correlation coefficient between the predicted activation and the true activations for 60 dataset examples made up of nine tokens each, resulting in 540 predictions per feature. While only using completely random sequences would be the most principled approach to scoring, half of the examples are from across the feature intervals to get a more accurate correlation.
claims.location: Global Analysis > Automated Interpretability - Activations; Appendix > Automated Interpretability > Experimental Setup

claims.planned: The automated activation-prediction scores for features vs neurons (specific median correlations)
claims.finding: The text states only that Claude explains and predicts activations 'significantly better' for features than for neurons; the actual score distributions are in a figure that is not present in the extracted text. Do not cite a median correlation value from this page.
claims.quote: In agreement with the human analysis, Claude is able to explain and predict activations for features significantly better than for neurons. In instances where Claude predicts a constant score, most often all 0s, a correlation can't be computed and we assign a score of zero which explains the uptick there.

claims.planned: A second held-out test uses the explanation to predict which output tokens the feature should promote (logit weights): 74% for features vs 58% for neurons, chance 50%
claims.finding: Averages 74% (features) vs 58% (neurons); medians 0.74 vs 0.53 vs 0.5 for a randomized transformer. Scored against a 50/50 mix of top positive logit tokens (ranks 10-60, since the top 10 were used for the explanation and so held out) and random tokens.
claims.quote: Randomly guessing would give a 50% accuracy, but the model instead achieves a 74% average across features, compared to a 58% average across neurons. ... The A/1 features are quite a bit better than the neurons at a median of 0.74 versus 0.53 for the neurons and 0.5 for the randomized transformer.
claims.location: Global Analysis > Automated Interpretability - Logit Weights; Appendix > Automated Interpretability

claims.planned: A randomized-transformer control exists, and it exposed a weakness of the automated activation score: features of a random network scored higher on it
claims.finding: Features learned on a transformer with random weights serve as a control. Logit-weight prediction sits at chance for it, and manual scoring favors the real features, but the automated activation score gave the randomized features a higher median, because many of them are pure single-token features that are trivially simulable.
claims.quote: As a further ablation, we compare our human and automated interpretability approaches to the randomized transformer. It is unsurprising that the logit weight predictions are centered around random chance for the randomized transformer by the very nature of its random weights. Manual interpretability also favors the A/1 features. However, for automated interpretability the randomized features have a higher median score. It turns out that the randomized transformer features are distinctly bimodal, consisting of single token and polysemantic clusters ... The single token features of the randomized transformer are not only more numerous but also more truly single token

teachable_points.point: Evaluate across the whole activation range, not just the top: polysemanticity hides below the top examples.
teachable_points.quote: Many polysemantic neurons appear monosemantic if you only look at top dataset examples, but are revealed to be polysemantic if you look at lower parts of the activation spectrum.
teachable_points.numbers: 11 activation intervals; 412 intervals scored over 162 features and neurons; median neuron 0, median feature interval 12.

teachable_points.point: A control that should score badly and does not is a finding about the metric: a random network's features out-scored real ones on automated activation prediction because single-token features are trivially predictable.
teachable_points.quote: for automated interpretability the randomized features have a higher median score
teachable_points.numbers: logit-weight prediction medians: 0.74 features, 0.53 neurons, 0.5 randomized.
